questions.passage: Coral reefs cover less than one per cent of the ocean floor, yet they are home to around a quarter of all marine species. They also protect coastlines from storms and support the fishing and tourism industries in many countries. Unfortunately, reefs are under serious threat. When sea temperatures rise, corals lose the tiny algae that live inside them and give them their colour, a process known as bleaching. If temperatures return to normal quickly, corals can recover, but repeated bleaching often kills them. Scientists are experimenting with ways to help, such as growing heat-resistant corals in nurseries and replanting them on damaged reefs, but they agree that reducing global warming remains essential.
